response.evidence: An analysis of the data shows that loan approvals and denials are distributed across all demographic groups, including race, ethnicity, gender, and age. Denials consistently correlate with financial risk factors—such as high debt-to-income ratios (e.g., >50%) or high loan-to-value ratios—across these groups, rather than showing a disproportionate or systematic bias against any specific protected class.

The data shows that loan decisions are driven by financial risk metrics rather than demographic characteristics. Application denials are consistently associated with high Debt-to-Income (DTI) ratios (e.g., >60%) or very high Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratios across all racial, ethnic, and gender groups. Both minority and non-minority applicants (including White non-Hispanic applicants) experience denials when presenting risky financial profiles, and both groups are routinely approved when presenting healthy metrics, indicating no systemic bias or discrimination in the underwriting process.

The data does not show evidence of discrimination based on race, ethnicity, or gender. Loan denials are consistently associated with high financial risk factors, such as high debt-to-income (DTI) ratios (e.g., >60% or 50%-60%) and high loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, across all demographic groups. Conversely, applicants from various minority and protected classes (including Black, Asian, Hispanic, and female applicants) frequently had their loans originated when their financial metrics were within acceptable limits, demonstrating that decisions were driven by objective financial criteria rather than demographic bias.
